stances.claim: The Scotus's March 4 unsigned unanimous resolution overturning the Colorado Supreme Court is 'a major legal victory' for Trump, holding that only Congress (not state courts) has the power to enforce the 14th Amendment Section 3 ban -- and crucially 'skirted the main issue of whether Trump is an insurrectionist or a rebel.'

The Scotus 'left open' the question of what constitutes an 'insurrection' and what kind of implementing law Congress would need to pass -- five of nine justices in separate opinions argued the ban must be contained in a law, but passing such legislation before November 2024 is 'almost impossible' given the huge political chasm between Democratic-controlled Senate and Republican-controlled House.

Scotus ruled 'narrowly' to avoid Frankfurter's 'political thicket' -- preferring not to be directly involved in political controversies, much less to take out from the ballot a candidate who is 'the obvious choice of one of two major political parties' -- even using an unsigned resolution to avoid the constitutional certification requirement that PH would impose.
stances.rhetorical_move: judicial-shyness framing with PH-comparative procedural critique

stances.claim: PH's federal/centralized contrast: 'in contrast to the US federal system, ours is a unitary or centralized state' -- so there is no exact parallel to a state supreme court deciding federal-Constitution issues. The closest PH analog is that PH courts have no jurisdiction over federal-Constitution cases.

'This typical judicial shyness is, however, taboo in our country' because the PH Constitution mandates the SC with 'the duty, not just the power, to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion' -- placing the PH SC repeatedly 'in the vortex of political whirlpools.'
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-mandate contrast (PH grave-abuse-of-discretion as anti-shy clause)

stances.claim: Trump 'triumphantly waived' the Scotus decision as 'implied endorsement' and handily won 14 of 15 Super Tuesday states (Vermont excepted), forcing Nikki Haley to withdraw without the traditional graceful endorsement -- instead warning Republicans that 'chaos and personal grievance always follow Trump.'

Worth watching whether the Scotus will 'rule narrowly again and bury its head in the political sand' on Trump's presidential-immunity defense in pending federal cases -- including the New York court's $454M fraud fine.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Scotus's March 4, 2024 'unanimous unsigned resolution' overturning the Colorado Supreme Court's December 2023 4-3 ruling that had barred Donald Trump from the state's ballot under Section 3 of the 14th Amendment for his alleged 'insurrection or rebellion' role in the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol assault. Trump's victory -- among approximately 100 civil, criminal, and other cases pending against him -- turned on 'what laypersons call a technicality': the Scotus held that only Congress (not state courts) may enforce the constitutional ban, and pointedly 'skirted the main issue of whether Trump is an insurrectionist or a rebel.' Five of nine justices in separate opinions argued the ban must be contained in a law, but passing such legislation before November 2024 is 'almost impossible' given the chasm between the Democratic-controlled Senate and the Republican-controlled House -- reminiscent of similarly stalled PH Charter-change attempts. The Scotus also left open what constitutes an 'insurrection,' acknowledged state-court jurisdiction over state-office (not federal-office) candidates, and used an unsigned resolution that does not bear the kind of constitutional certification PH SC decisions must carry under our 1987 Constitution. CJ frames this as Scotus's 'rule narrowly' approach -- avoiding what 'the late conservative Justice Felix Frankfurter described as the political thicket' -- and contrasts it sharply with the PH SC, where 'this typical judicial shyness is, however, taboo' because our Constitution mandates 'the duty, not just the power, to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion,' placing the PH SC repeatedly 'in the vortex of political whirlpools' (foreshadowing A77 the following week). Whether by coincidence or design (?), the Scotus ruling was released on the eve of Super Tuesday, when Trump 'triumphantly waived' it as implied endorsement and handily won 14 of 15 states (Vermont excepted), forcing Nikki Haley to withdraw without the traditional endorsement -- instead warning MAGA Republicans that 'chaos and personal grievance always follow Trump.' CJ closes with the forward-projection: worth watching whether the Scotus will 'rule narrowly again and bury its head in the political sand' on Trump's presidential-immunity defense in pending federal cases -- including the New York court's $454 million fraud fine.
